India after the Second World War

The end of the Second World War in 1945 produced a difficult situation for the British government in India. Britain had incurred enormous wartime costs, while Indian society had experienced inflation, shortages and political repression. Wartime mobilisation had also expanded the number of Indians serving in the armed forces and working in war-related industries.

At the same time, the nationalist demand for independence was stronger than before. The British government had to consider whether colonial rule could be maintained politically, economically and militarily, and what arrangements would be necessary to transfer power.

The question of armed-forces loyalty

British rule in India depended heavily on Indian soldiers, sailors, police personnel and civil servants carrying out government orders. Loyalty in this context meant the willingness of personnel to continue serving and obeying the colonial chain of command.

The INA trials and the Royal Indian Navy uprising affected British assessments in different ways:

  • INA trials: Public sympathy for men who had fought against Britain showed that the wartime actions of some Indian soldiers could be viewed as patriotic rather than disloyal.
  • Naval uprising: Ratings serving within a British-controlled military institution openly challenged their superiors and attracted civilian support.
  • Wider political effect: These developments raised doubts about the long-term security of a political system that relied on Indian personnel to enforce colonial authority.

They did not establish that all Indian armed forces had stopped obeying British orders. Much of the military command structure remained effective, including during the suppression of the naval revolt.

Three distinct developments

The INA campaign was an overseas military attempt to end British rule. The INA trials were post-war prosecutions that produced nationalist protests. The RIN uprising was a revolt by serving naval ratings in February 1946. Their causes and dates differ, even though their political effects were connected.

Labour unrest in 1946

The naval uprising formed part of a broader period of industrial and public-service unrest. Workers demanded better wages and conditions in an economy affected by the war and rising prices.

The Bombay strike of 22 February 1946 was directly connected with support for the naval ratings. Other disputes had their own immediate economic causes. In July 1946, postal and telegraph workers went on strike over pay and service conditions. Railway employees also threatened industrial action during the year.

These examples should not be treated as one centrally organised movement. Together, however, they showed the colonial government that dissatisfaction affected several important services and could disrupt administration and economic activity.

The Cabinet Mission and constitutional negotiations

The British government was also pursuing a negotiated political settlement. On 19 February 1946, Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced in the British House of Commons that a mission of Cabinet ministers would go to India. The announcement followed the opening of the naval revolt on 18 February, but plans for political negotiations and elections had already been made in 1945.

The Cabinet Mission arrived in India in March 1946. Its members were Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander.

The mission sought an arrangement for transferring power and framing a constitution. Its proposals of 16 May 1946 envisaged a united India with a limited central government and groupings of provinces. Serious disagreements between Congress and the Muslim League, particularly over constitutional arrangements and political representation, prevented a lasting settlement.

The Cabinet Mission was an initiative of the British government. It was not a committee formed by the INA, the naval ratings or the Congress to investigate the mutiny.

From a fixed deadline to independence

On 20 February 1947, Attlee's government announced that it intended to transfer power to Indian hands by June 1948 at the latest. This was an announced deadline, not the date on which independence eventually occurred.

On 3 June 1947, the British government announced the plan that provided for the partition of British India and transfer of power to separate successor states. India became independent on 15 August 1947.

The transfer of power resulted from several connected developments: the long national movement, the weakened position of Britain after the war, pressure from political parties, mass mobilisation, questions about military reliability and the growing difficulty of securing agreement between Congress and the Muslim League.

The INA trials and the naval uprising contributed to this crisis by demonstrating the strength of nationalist feeling and the risks of continued colonial rule. They were important influences, but neither event alone explains why or exactly when Britain transferred power.

One chronological view of the final phase

The chronology makes one central distinction clear: Bose's Congress conflict preceded the INA's wartime campaign; the INA's defeat preceded its trials; the trials preceded the naval uprising; and all these developments occurred while Britain and Indian political leaders were negotiating the end of colonial rule.

Prelims focus

  • November 1945: First major INA Red Fort trial began.
  • 18–23 February 1946: Main Royal Indian Navy uprising.
  • 19 February 1946: British government announced the Cabinet Mission.
  • March 1946: Cabinet Mission arrived in India; proposals followed on 16 May 1946.
  • 20 February 1947: Britain announced a deadline of June 1948 for transferring power.
  • 3 June and 15 August 1947: Partition plan announced; India subsequently attained independence.
  • Trap: June 1948 was the announced latest deadline, whereas independence actually came on 15 August 1947.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed pp. 123–125, consulted in the GPSC Books compendium; Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 19, sections 19.2, 19.3 and 19.4.1, printed pp. 259–274; UK Parliament, Hansard, House of Commons, 'India (Cabinet Ministers' Mission)', 19 February 1946, vol. 419, cols. 964–966; UK Parliament, Hansard, House of Commons, 'India (Transfer of Power)', 3 June 1947; Government of India archival material, Ministry of External Affairs, appendix 'The Cabinet Mission', statement and arrival details; historical sources consulted 22 November 2026.]
